key_facts: UK and EU agreed a deal covering removal of most checks on British food exports in exchange for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, linking of UK and EU emissions trading systems (aim to apply from 2028), and a youth experience scheme allowing up to 100,000 18–31 year olds from each side to travel, work and study for up to three years, with opportunities available by no later than January 2030.

The UK Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year; Burnham said it will add up to 0.5% to UK GDP, which Badenoch disputed. Talks on tuition fees for students are to continue for a further six months.

Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week. Burnham said the UK government will publish a 10-year plan next month, and that the deal is probably the limit of what can be achieved in this Parliament.

Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged no return to the single market, customs union, or freedom of movement; Burnham has committed to this. Critics argue the food-check changes make the UK a 'rule taker' rather than a rule maker.
importance_reason: Formal UK–EU post-Brexit reset agreement with quantified economic impact claims and direct effects on food trade and emissions trading from 2028.
market_link: Removal of food export checks and linking of UK and EU emissions trading systems could affect UK–EU trade costs, carbon prices and sterling sentiment; the £17bn/0.5% GDP estimate is disputed, so the size of any macro effect is uncertain.
